findings.piece: Calculator: option labels, and no input for an inadequate sequence
findings.says: DWI options "2 — Indistinct hypointensity on ADC", "3 — Focal mild/moderate hypointensity; <1.5 cm"; T2WI options "1 — Normal TZ or round well-defined BPH nodule", "2 — Circumscribed hypointense, well-defined margins"; DCE "Yes — Focal early enhancement" (hint "PZ only: focal early enhancement vs. adjacent tissue"). All four fields are required; none has an option for a sequence that is technically inadequate or not done, and the T2WI hint says it is "not used for PZ scoring".
findings.fix: Relabel the options with v2.1's wording (DWI 3 has no size limit in either version; a T2W 1 nodule is completely encapsulated, whatever its signal; DCE+ must match a T2W/DWI finding). Add "inadequate / not done" for DWI and DCE that applies the p. 16 tables (without adequate DWI, PZ and TZ are scored on T2W, with DCE+ raising 3 to 4).
findings.recheckNote: agrees — The DWI 2 and 3 labels are the v2 wording that v2.1 replaced, and "<1.5 cm" on DWI 3 is in neither version (size appears only at scores 4 and 5). T2W 2 is the v2 wording; T2W 1 "round well-defined BPH nodule" drops v2.1's "completely encapsulated" (a circumscribed nodule without a capsule is score 2). There is no "X" option, so the v2.1 tables for inadequate DWI or DCE cannot be applied; in those tables T2W does score the PZ and DCE does act in the TZ (T2W 3, DWI X), so the hints "not used for PZ scoring" and "PZ only" hold only when all sequences are adequate. The DCE label omits that the enhancement must correspond to a suspicious T2W/DWI finding. findings.piece: DCE role (PZ): what counts as positive and negative
findings.says: "DCE positive: Focal early enhancement (earlier than or simultaneously with adjacent normal tissue), used to upgrade DWI score 3 → PI-RADS 4"; "DCE negative: Does not change the DWI assessment".
findings.fix: Define a positive DCE by all three conditions (focal; earlier than or with adjacent normal tissue; matching a suspicious T2W/DWI finding) and list v2.1's negatives, including focal enhancement of a BPH-type nodule extruded into the PZ, which must not upgrade a DWI 3.
findings.recheckNote: disagreed — Reviewer: correct (management). Focal, earlier than or contemporaneous, and the 3 → 4 upgrade in the PZ are right; a negative DCE leaves the DWI score. The page leaves out the third condition (the enhancement must correspond to a suspicious T2W and/or DWI finding) and that focal enhancement in a lesion with BPH features counts as negative. (pirads-2-1, Section IV C, p. 22 (PDF p. 29) and C.2 table; Section III, p. 10) Resolution: Stands as wrong with management: the omitted third condition (enhancement matching a suspicious T2W/DWI finding) and v2.1's negatives (a BPH-type nodule extruded into the PZ) are what stop a false DWI 3 → 4 upgrade, so the gap changes the category (DCE section, pp. 21–22).

(pirads-2-1, Caveats for Overall Assessment, pp. 14–15 (PDF pp. 21–22); Section IV B, p. 19; Appendix I template) Resolution: Stands as wrong: the list is mixed, but "don't assign PI-RADS based on a single sequence" contradicts the dominant-sequence rule (pp. 14–15: the category comes from DWI in the PZ, T2W in the TZ), and the anterior-tumour line inverts the document's advice on high b-value DWI (p. 19).

findings.fix: Add ACR's limits: number and label each followed nodule, follow at most four (highest points) below the FNA threshold, and biopsy at most two (highest points, not the largest). Gland size and echogenicity are not in the white paper.

findings.question: Which should lead each contrast topic? By the audit rule: CAR/CSACI 2025 for hypersensitivity and premedication, CAR 2022 for contrast-associated AKI and metformin, CAR 2018/2019 for gadolinium in kidney disease (copies requested from you), and the ACR Manual for reaction treatment, extravasation, pregnancy, breast-feeding and the thyroid. findings.piece: Adverse Reaction Classification, "Acute Reactions (within 1 hour)" tab: timing and severity grades (Severity and Symptoms columns)
findings.says: "Acute Reactions (within 1 hour)"; "Mild | Limited urticaria, nausea/vomiting, pruritus, pallor/diaphoresis"; "Moderate | Diffuse urticaria, mild bronchospasm, facial edema, tachycardia/bradycardia"; "Severe | Diffuse bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, anaphylactic shock, cardiac arrest".
findings.fix: Use the ACR grades as CAR/CSACI reproduce them, with allergic-like and physiologic reactions apart: facial edema is moderate only without dyspnea (with dyspnea, severe); bronchospasm is graded by hypoxia; "pallor/diaphoresis" and "tachycardia/bradycardia" are not grades in the source (hypotension with bradycardia is vasovagal, with tachycardia anaphylactic shock). The 1-hour window is right.
findings.recheckNote: disagreed — Reviewer: wrong. The 1-hour window (CAR/CSACI: 'Acute or immediate HRs occur within 1 hour') and most entries match, but 'pallor/diaphoresis' (mild) and 'tachycardia/bradycardia' (moderate) are not in ACR Table 1, which CAR/CSACI reproduces as Appendix A. The page also drops the allergic-like versus physiologic split and the qualifiers that set the grade (facial edema 'without dyspnea', bronchospasm graded by hypoxia). (acr-contrast-2024, Table 1 Categories of Acute Reactions, printed p 95-96 (PDF p 98-99); car-csaci-hypersensitivity-2025, Physiology and Classification, p 2, and Appendix A) Resolution: Stands with management: the grade decides the treatment, and the page drops the qualifiers that set it (facial edema "without dyspnea", bronchospasm graded by hypoxia) — ACR Table 1, reproduced as CAR/CSACI Appendix A.

sources.location: Table 1, Categories of Acute Reactions, pp95–96 (PDF pp98–99): mild allergic-like — limited urticaria/pruritis, cutaneous edema, limited "itchy"/"scratchy" throat, nasal congestion, sneezing/conjunctivitis/rhinorrhea; mild physiologic — limited nausea/vomiting, transient flushing/warmth/chills, headache/dizziness/anxiety/altered taste, mild hypertension, vasovagal reaction that resolves spontaneously. Moderate allergic-like — diffuse urticaria/pruritis, diffuse erythema with stable vital signs, facial edema without dyspnea, throat tightness or hoarseness without dyspnea, wheezing/bronchospasm with mild or no hypoxia; moderate physiologic — protracted nausea/vomiting, hypertensive urgency, isolated chest pain, vasovagal reaction that requires and is responsive to treatment. findings.piece: Adverse Reaction Classification, "Acute Reactions" tab: Treatment column

findings.fix: Moderate bronchospasm starts with a beta-agonist inhaler (albuterol), adding epinephrine if needed; severe reactions with hypotension take IV epinephrine (0.1 mg of 0.1 mg/mL) when there is IV access, IM 0.3 mg otherwise. Mild: observe 20–30 minutes; an oral antihistamine if symptomatic (CAR/CSACI: second-generation).
findings.recheckNote: disagreed — Reviewer: correct (management). A fair but thin summary. It leaves out the beta-agonist inhaler, which the ACR gives first for moderate bronchospasm before considering epinephrine, and for hypotensive patients the ACR prefers IV epinephrine (IM if no IV access). (acr-contrast-2024, Table 3 (hives p 104, bronchospasm p 106, hypotension p 108; PDF p 107, 109, 111) and Treatment of Contrast Reactions p 86 (PDF p 89)) Resolution: Stands as wrong with management: re-read ACR Table 3 — for anaphylaxis with hypotension the ACR's first choice is epinephrine IV (IM only without IV access), and moderate bronchospasm starts with the beta-agonist inhaler; the page's quick-reference column, the part read mid-reaction, gives severe reactions IM only and skips the inhaler.

findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: gadolinium items
findings.says: Don't: "Use Group I/II GBCA agents in patients with eGFR <30 when alternatives exist"; Do: "Choose macrocyclic GBCA when renal function is compromised".
findings.fix: Against ACR 2024, Group II is the recommended group at eGFR <30, so "don't use Group I/II" is wrong (Group I alone is right) and the choice is Group II rather than "macrocyclic". The verdict waits for CAR 2018/2019.

The 'Do' is close but not the ACR's rule: it prefers Group II agents, which include the linear agents gadobenate and gadoxetate, rather than 'macrocyclic' as such. findings.piece: Common Pitfalls: renal function and metformin items
findings.says: Don't: "Routinely hold metformin for eGFR ≥30 (outdated practice)"; Do: "Check eGFR and relevant medications before contrast".
findings.fix: Replace "check eGFR before contrast" with CAR's screen: eGFR for inpatients (within 7 days) or when the screening questions are positive, never delaying emergent studies; metformin is the only drug held (eGFR ≤30 or AKI), and it continues at eGFR >30, not ≥30.
findings.recheckNote: disagreed — Reviewer: correct (management). Not routinely holding metformin above eGFR 30 matches CAR (which holds at exactly 30) and the ACR. 'Check eGFR before contrast' is broader than either source: CAR screens stable outpatients with a two-question questionnaire and proceeds without an eGFR when the answers are no, and says emergent imaging should not wait for one. (car-ca-aki-2022, Summary of recommendations, recommendations 1 and 16; acr-contrast-2024, PC-AKI chapter, Screening, printed p 38 (PDF p 41)) Resolution: Stands as not-lead with management: CAR 2022 screens stable outpatients with a two-question questionnaire and says emergent imaging should not wait for an eGFR; a blanket "check eGFR before contrast" can delay emergency studies.
